newsitem.title: UK: Moody's confirms BTR units Prime-1 CP rating.
newsitem.headline: Moody's confirms BTR units Prime-1 CP rating.

text.p: Moody's said on Friday it confirmed its Prime-1 ratings for commercial paper of BTR Dunlop Finance Inc and BTR Finance (Guernsey) Ltd, whose obligations are guaranteed by their ultimate parent, BTR Plc.
"The confirmation follows BTR's announcement of a significant restructuring charge as the group continues to refocus on core engineering and manufacturing businesses," Moody's said in a statement.

Moody's said the confirmation recognised that a significant element of the charge is a non-cash provision related to businesses to be divested rather than a change in the economic value of the core business portfolio.

"The rating action anticipates that BTR will be able to generate stronger growth by concentrating on its selected ongoing businesses and limit its reliance on debt-financed acquisitions," the agency said.

It said BTR planed to reconfigure its thirty-two product groups into seven business groups and continue the process of rationalisation started with the purchase of the minority in BTR-Nylex at the end of 1995.

"Disposals representing approximately 25 percent of BTR group sales during 1995 have been made or are planned to be made by the end of 1997 but the group will still retain scale and leading market positions in a number of businesses and continues to benefit from a significant degree of diversity," Moody's said.
Moody's said the group's focus on companies which generate high returns on their operating assets was strategically sound.

"While...difficult market conditions in certain of BTR's business sectors, in particular automotive, could temper organic growth in relevant businesses, new market opportunities and related moderate size acquisitions should support higher profits from the overall rebased group during the intermediate term," Moody's said.
"Consequently, debt protection should strengthen as improved cash flow and disposal proceeds reduce debt and lower dividends enable equity to build during the intermediate term," it said.
Moody's noted that over half of the exceptional charge before taxation is non cash with approximately 40 percent related to book write-downs of assets to be disposed.
"The lower dividend payout and cash pay back periods soften the impact of cash based rationalisation costs," Moody's said.
